**The Moon Keeper**

Sam was sitting by his bedroom window. His knees were pulled up to his chest. His nose was pressed close to the cool glass.

"What are you watching for, Sam?" asked Dad, from the doorway.

"The moon," said Sam. "What if it forgets to come up tonight?"

Dad came in quietly. He sat down on the edge of the bed. "That is a big worry," he said. "It makes sense that you feel it."

Sam nodded. His chin wobbled a little. "It gets so dark. Then I can't see anything. I feel all alone in the dark."

"Lots of children feel that way," said Dad. "Dark can feel very big when you are small."

Sam looked out at the sky. It was full of tiny lights. Some were stars. Some were just dim, far-away sparkles.

"Shall we keep watch together?" asked Dad. "Just for a little while."

So they did. Dad put his arm around Sam. They sat together by the window and waited.

"Let's try something," said Dad. "Breathe in slowly, like you are smelling a flower. Then breathe out slowly, like you are blowing out a candle. Want to try?"

Sam breathed in. He breathed out. "Again," he said softly.

They breathed together. In, and out. In, and out.

Down the street, a dog barked once and then was quiet. Sam's shoulders came down a little.

"There," whispered Dad. "Look at that cloud."

A soft gray cloud was drifting across the sky. Its edges glowed silver, as if someone had brushed them with light.

Then, slowly, the moon began to rise over the rooftops. It was round and pale and calm. It did not hurry. It did not stop. It simply came up, the way it always had.

"Oh," breathed Sam. "It came."

"It always comes," said Dad. "Every night. Even when we cannot see it, it is still there, moving along, doing its work."

Sam smiled. He leaned against Dad's arm. "I feel a little less scared now."

"That is good," said Dad. "You can keep breathing slowly, whenever you need. And you can look for the moon any time, or just hold your soft bunny close."

Sam reached for Bunny, who was sitting on the windowsill. He tucked it under his chin.

The moon climbed higher, soft and steady. Its light spilled gently across the floor and over the blankets.

Sam's eyes grew heavy. His breathing slowed. In, and out. In, and out.

"Good night, moon," he mumbled.

Dad lifted him gently and carried him to bed. He tucked the blanket up under Sam's chin. Bunny was tucked in right beside him.

"Good night, Sam," whispered Dad. "The moon is keeping watch. And so am I."

The window glowed silver. The room was quiet. Sam was warm, and safe, and fast asleep.

versions.text:
Milo and the Brave Bedtime

Milo lived in a small blue house with a big yellow door. His bedroom had a window, a bookshelf, and a bed with a green blanket. On the bed sat his favorite stuffed rabbit, named Biscuit.

Tonight Milo sat up in bed. His eyes were wide. "Mama," he whispered, "tomorrow I start at a new school."

Mama sat down beside him. "That sounds big," she said. "Tell me how you feel."

"I feel wobbly," said Milo. "My tummy goes flip-flop. And the dark feels bigger when I think about it."

Mama nodded. "That makes sense. New things can feel big. And it's okay to feel wobbly. Lots of children feel that way."

Milo hugged Biscuit tight. "Biscuit feels wobbly too," he said.

Mama smiled. "Let's help Biscuit feel better. Maybe you could practice saying hello. Biscuit is very good at listening."

Milo sat up a little straighter. He held Biscuit up to his face. "Hello," he said softly. "My name is Milo."

"Hello, Milo," said Mama, in a funny rabbit voice. "I am Biscuit. I like your blanket."

Milo giggled. "Thank you," he said. "Hello. I like to draw dinosaurs."

They practiced again. And again. Each time Milo's voice got a little stronger. The flip-flop in his tummy got a little smaller.

Then Milo looked at the window. The moon was round and silver. Outside, the trees were still.

"The dark still feels a little big," he said quietly.

Mama reached over and turned on the little star lamp by the bed. Soft, gold light spread across the blanket. "Now there's a little light to keep you company," she said. "Your room looks just like your room, see? Your books. Your toy truck. Biscuit is right here."

Milo looked around. The bookshelf was still there. The toy truck was still there. Everything was in its place.

"Oh," he said. "It's still my room."

"It always is," said Mama. "And I'll be right down the hall, all night long."

Milo took a deep breath in. He let it out slowly, like blowing on warm soup. He did it once more. Then once more after that.

"Mama," he said, "when I feel wobbly at school, I can take a slow breath. And I can say hello to a new friend. Like practicing with Biscuit."

"That's a wonderful plan," said Mama. "You know just what to do."

Milo tucked Biscuit under his arm. He pulled the green blanket up to his chin. His eyes felt heavy and soft.

"Good night, Mama," he murmured.

"Good night, Milo," said Mama. She kissed his forehead. "Sweet dreams."

The star lamp glowed. The moon kept watch through the window. Milo breathed slowly, in and out, in and out. Biscuit sat close by his cheek.

Tomorrow was a new day. But tonight, Milo was safe, warm, and ready to rest.

versions.text:
Milo and the Letter Under the Pillow

Milo lay in his cozy bed. The room was dark. The night-light glowed, soft and yellow.

Milo was sad. His best friend, Sam, had moved far away. Sam lived in a city across the big river now.

"I miss Sam," Milo said quietly.

His mom sat on the edge of the bed. She stroked his hair. "I know, sweetheart. It is hard when a friend goes far away."

"It feels like the dark is bigger without him," Milo whispered. "Sometimes I feel scared of the dark, and I don't have Sam to tell."

Mom did not laugh. She did not say, "Don't be silly." She nodded slowly. "Being scared and missing someone are both real feelings. You are allowed to have them. Let's think of something together."

Milo sat up. He looked at his blanket, which was blue and soft.

"I could write Sam a letter," he said. "Then I wouldn't feel so alone."

"That is a lovely idea," said Mom.

So Milo found a pencil and a piece of paper. He wrote slowly, in big letters.

*Dear Sam, I miss you. Remember the tree house? Let's build a new one when you come back. Your friend, Milo.*

He read it twice. Then he folded it into a small square.

"Can I keep it under my pillow?" he asked.

"Of course," said Mom. "Then it will be close to you all night."

Milo tucked the letter under his pillow. He felt a little warmer inside.

Mom took a slow breath, in and out. "When the dark feels big, you can breathe like this with me. In through the nose. Out through the mouth. Want to try?"

Milo nodded. They breathed together. In, and out. In, and out.

Milo's hand found the soft edge of his blanket. He held it tight, then let it go. He looked at the night-light. It glowed like a little moon.

"The dark is still there," Milo said.

"It is," said Mom. "But you are here, and I am here, and the letter is here too."

Milo smiled. The room did not feel so big now.

Mom kissed his forehead. "I'll leave the door open a little. Goodnight, Milo."

"Goodnight, Mom," Milo mumbled.

Milo closed his eyes. He pictured Sam standing by the big oak tree. Sam waved and grinned. Together they climbed up and up, and the wooden planks of their new tree house creaked happily under their feet. The wind hummed a gentle song. The river sparkled far below, calm and blue.

"Next time," Sam called softly, "we will build the best tree house ever."

Milo yawned. His breathing slowed. His blanket felt heavy and warm.

Under his pillow, the letter rested quietly, keeping its promise.

The night-light glowed on. The house was still. Milo was safe, cozy and sleepy, and his dream drifted on like a boat on a calm sea until morning.
